opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the questions I find most interesting. The striking fact is that a large language model trains on something like tens of trillions of tokens, while a human child gets to fluent language on maybe tens or hundreds of millions of words. That's several orders of magnitude. So the natural question is: where does that gap come from, and is it fundamental?

I think there are a few pieces, and it's easy to conflate them.

First, humans aren't starting from scratch. Evolution has run an enormous outer-loop optimization over hundreds of millions of years, and what comes out is a brain with a lot of structure already baked in: inductive biases, architecture, maybe some priors about objects, agents, causality. So when you compare a child to a model trained from random initialization, it isn't apples to apples. In some sense the "pretraining" for humans happened over evolutionary time, and the child is doing something closer to fine-tuning.

Second, the data is very different. A child isn't passively reading text. They're embodied and interacting with the world. They run experiments, push things off tables, see what happens, get feedback from parents. That's active, multimodal, and highly correlated with their own actions. Text on the internet is a compressed, lossy record of human experience, and the model has to back out the world from it indirectly. Arguably it's remarkable it works at all.

Third, the question I care about as a physicist: is there something about the learning algorithm itself, or the scale, that explains the difference? In theory work on deep learning, a lot of what we find is that these networks are, in some sense, simple. They behave in ways describable by effective theories, and their sample efficiency is tied to their inductive biases and how they represent the data. Scaling laws tell you how loss improves with data and parameters, but they don't tell you the constant out front is optimal. There's no reason to think current architectures and training procedures sit at some fundamental limit. The scaling exponents might be the thing to change, not just how far we push along the curve.

And there's an interesting twist: once models are large and pretrained, they become quite sample-efficient. In-context learning is a good example. Give a big model a few examples and it picks up a new task immediately, which looks a lot more like how humans learn. So the inefficiency is concentrated in the pretraining phase, which, again, is maybe more analogous to evolution plus early development than to a person learning something new as an adult.

So my view is that the gap is real, but it's partly a measurement artifact from comparing the wrong things, and partly a genuine signal that there's a lot of room to improve. Understanding which part is which is exactly where theory should help. If we understood why these systems learn the way they do, we'd have a much better sense of whether we can close that gap by being clever rather than just by spending more compute.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts models trained on tens of trillions of tokens with children reaching fluent language after tens or hundreds of millions of words, conveying far less human exposure.

r002.rationale: It explains that humans have evolved inductive biases and learn through embodied, interactive experience, unlike models trained on text, making their learning processes substantially different.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I think about a lot, because it's one of those things where, if you look at the numbers, the gap is kind of astonishing. A human, by the time they're twenty, has seen on the order of maybe a hundred million words, maybe a billion if you're being generous. And a frontier language model is trained on tens of trillions of tokens. So you're talking about four or five orders of magnitude more data to get to something that's, in some ways comparable, and in a lot of ways still worse at the things we care about.

I think the first thing to say is that the comparison is a little unfair in both directions. The model is learning everything from scratch, from random initialization. A human comes with a few hundred million years of evolution baked into the architecture. So some of what looks like sample efficiency in humans is really that the prior is extremely good. You could think of evolution as a very long, very expensive pretraining run, and we don't usually count that against us when we're doing the accounting.

But I don't think that fully explains it. The other piece, which I find more interesting from a physics perspective, is that the way we train these models is almost deliberately wasteful. We take a fixed dataset, we shuffle it, and we do gradient descent on next-token prediction with a learning rate that's basically the same for every token. There's no mechanism for the model to say, this part is surprising, I should think about it harder, and this part I already know, let me move on. Humans do that constantly. You read something confusing, you stop, you reread, you connect it to things you already know. That's a very different kind of learning dynamics, and I think a lot of the efficiency gap is actually living in that.

And then there's a third thing, which is that the data itself is different. A human's data is embodied and interactive. You act, the world responds, and the signal you get is directly about the thing you did. Text on the internet is just a very lossy projection of that. So the model is trying to reconstruct a world model from shadows on the wall, and it's not surprising that takes a lot more shadows.

What I'd love to understand, and what I think we're still fairly far from understanding theoretically, is how those factors decompose. Like, if you could actually attribute the five orders of magnitude, how much is prior, how much is the learning algorithm, how much is the data modality. My guess is the learning algorithm piece is bigger than people assume, and that's the one we actually have levers on.

r001.rationale: The response compares the amount of human exposure with model training data, but does not state that humans learn to speak in sentences.

r002.rationale: The response explains that humans and models differ in their built-in priors, learning dynamics, and data, and links those differences to the efficiency gap.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real gap, but it’s tricky to make the comparison precise. A human can learn a new concept from a handful of examples, whereas a language model might need an enormous amount of training data. But that human isn’t starting from scratch. They bring years of experience, and a brain whose structure reflects a very long evolutionary process.

There’s also a question of what we’re counting as data. A child isn’t just hearing words. They’re seeing things, touching them, taking actions, and observing consequences. That’s a very different learning setup from reading text. And they can actively seek out the experience that resolves their uncertainty.

So I’d separate two questions: How much experience does it take to build a broadly capable learner? And once you have that learner, how quickly can it pick up something new? Language models can sometimes do the second surprisingly well—you give them a few examples in context and they adapt. The first is where the enormous training cost sits.

To me, the interesting question is which parts of the human advantage come from prior structure, which come from richer experience, and which come from the learning process itself. Those imply quite different ways of closing the gap.

r001.rationale: It compares learning a new concept from a handful of examples with enormous model training data, but does not say humans learn to speak in sentences after exposure to fewer tokens.

r002.rationale: It explains that humans bring prior experience, learn through richer sensory and interactive experiences, and can seek information, while models incur large training costs—differences that explain why an efficiency gap can arise.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real gap, but it’s surprisingly hard to make a clean comparison. A human can learn a new concept from one or two examples, whereas a language model might be trained on trillions of tokens. That looks enormously inefficient. But the human isn’t starting from scratch. You’re bringing years of experience, and a brain whose structure has been shaped by evolution. How do you account for that prior information?

There’s also a difference in what the learner gets to do. Humans interact with the world. We choose what to look at, try things, and get feedback. A language model’s pretraining is largely learning from a fixed collection of observations. A child’s experience and a token of text aren’t really comparable units of training data.

Still, I wouldn’t use those caveats to explain the gap away. Humans seem remarkably good at identifying the structure of a problem and transferring it to a new situation. Models can do that too, especially when you give them examples in context, but it’s less reliable. The interesting question is which ingredients make that learning efficient: the architecture, the learning objective, prior experience, or the ability to actively gather useful information. I suspect it’s some combination, rather than one missing trick.

r001.rationale: The response compares learning a new concept from one or two examples with model training on trillions of tokens, but it does not state that humans learn to speak in sentences after exposure to fewer tokens.

r002.rationale: The response explains that humans bring prior experience and interact with the world, while language models largely learn from fixed observations, making direct comparisons difficult and the efficiency gap unsurprising.
